title: Examples of Rebirth in the Pure Land
excerpt: Master Tanxu says in his Instructions at the Seven-Day Buddha-Recitation Retreat:

inline.s: The power of a good example is boundless.

blocks.text: Master Tanxu on Rebirth in the Pure Land

inline.s: Master Tanxu says in his Instructions at the Seven-Day Buddha-Recitation Retreat:

At that time Master Dixian (that is, the Dharma Master Dixian, Master Tanxu's own teacher) had not yet made a name for himself. He was about forty and served as guest-prefect at Guanzong Monastery. In the last years of the Qing dynasty education was undeveloped and there were only family schools, so most children never studied. Master Dixian's family was comfortably off, so he had a few years of schooling and then went into business with his maternal uncle. In his youth he had a childhood friend in his hometown (a "childhood friend" means a companion and close friend from childhood). This friend's family was poor, he had never been to school, and he had learned the trade of a bowl-mender (in Beijing such a man is called a bowl-sawyer, that is, a mender of bowls: he clamps the broken pieces together with copper staples so that the bowl can still be used). His life was hard and he felt the bitterness of human existence deeply, so he went to Master Dixian and asked to leave home. Master Dixian said to him: "Do not make trouble for me. If you cannot read, you cannot study the scriptures, and being older you certainly cannot learn the five daily recitations or the chanting for Buddhist ceremonies. You had better go home and go back to business." He refused to give in, and in the end it was agreed that he would follow Master Dixian's conditions exactly. Master Dixian then shaved his head for him, instructing him not to take the precepts and not to live in a monastery: knowing nothing at all, he would be looked at coldly and life would be hard. He told him to live in a small temple in the countryside, to find a few lay supporters to provide him with the barest living, and to have an old lady who practiced Buddhism cook him two meals a day. And he taught him: "Recite the one line Namo Amitabha Buddha, and keep reciting it. When you are tired, rest a while, and when you have rested, recite again. In the future there will surely be benefit." He never asked what the benefit would be, and Master Dixian never told him.

In that small temple he recited the one Buddha-name to the very end. He recited for about three years and never went out. One day he went to visit a friend, and when he came back in the evening he said to the old lady: "Don't cook for me tomorrow." She did not ask why, thinking that someone would probably invite him to a meal. The next day after the noon meal the old lady grew uneasy and came to the temple to look. Entering the master's room, she saw him standing, facing the window, a rosary in one hand, the other hand smudged with ash. Looking closely, she saw that he had already passed away. She notified the lay supporters at once. When Master Dixian learned of it he hurried over. Seeing the scene, he praised him warmly and said: "After all, you did not leave home in vain. In your attainment, the great Dharma masters who expound the scriptures and the abbots and resident masters of famous mountains and precious monasteries are not your equal." Later they found eight or nine silver dollars in his hand. They were probably savings from his former business days, and his purpose was to ask his fellow practitioners to arrange his funeral: even after death he did not want to trouble anyone.
In his Treatise on Buddha-Recitation, Master Tanxu says:

As for those who attained rebirth through Buddha-recitation, whether monastic or lay, men or women, old or young, the various auspicious signs at the end of their lives have all been recorded in the Biographies of Rebirth, and such examples are too many to count. Since my own leaving home, I have seen more than twenty with my own eyes, not counting those I have only heard of. Now, to awaken everyone's faith, I will take three that I saw myself as examples.

The first was the monk Xiuwu, who had left home. He was from Yingkou and came from a family of brickmakers. Because his circumstances were poor and he found the work too hard, and because he felt that in this world of ours there is only suffering and no joy, he often thought about a way out of suffering. Later he heard people say that Buddha-recitation was good, and he resolved to recite the Buddha's name constantly. After leaving home and hearing the Buddhadharma properly, his resolve to recite grew more earnest, and whenever he met anyone he would urge them to recite as well.
In the eighteenth year of the Republic (

), I was at Jile Monastery in Harbin, in the Northeast, and had invited the old Dharma Master Dixian to come and transmit the precepts. One day a monk from the outer quarters came to me and said: "A certain Master Xiuwu has come from Yingkou and wishes to devote himself to austerities during the precept period." Later he brought him to see me. I asked him what he could do, and he said: "I wish to devote myself to nursing the sick." At that time Master Dingxi was prior at Jile Monastery, and he found him a room in the outer quarters. After staying a little over ten days he came to me again and said he wanted to leave. Master Dingxi, who was standing by, said: "You came with the resolve to nurse the sick; why do you want to leave after only ten days or so? That hardly shows constancy!" Master Xiuwu said: "I am not going anywhere else. I am going to be reborn. Please, Prior, be so kind as to prepare a few hundred catties of firewood, so that I may be cremated after death." Master Dingxi asked him: "When are you going?" Master Xiuwu said: "Within ten days." After saying this he went back to his own room. The next day he came to me and Master Dingxi again and said: "I take my leave of you, Dharma masters. I am going today. Please find me a room, and find a few people to recite the Buddha's name and see me off." Master Dingxi had a room in the public burial ground cleaned out, found a few planks and made up a bed, and then went to the outer quarters to find several monks to recite the Buddha's name and see him off. As the time of his rebirth drew near, those who had come to see him off said: "Master Xiuwu, today you are to be reborn in the Buddha-land. Before you go you should at least write a few lines of poetry or a gatha to leave as a keepsake." Master Xiuwu said: "I come from hard labor and have been dull since birth; I can neither write poems nor compose gathas. But I do have one saying born of experience that I can pass on to you all, namely:
To be able to speak but not to practice
(that is, to speak of faith and vows with the lips while doing nothing to prove that faith or fulfill those vows)
, is not true wisdom.

" Everyone who heard him say this found it very solid and true, and so they all recited the Buddha's name in unison. Master Xiuwu sat cross-legged facing west and recited along with them. In less than a quarter of an hour he passed away. The community hastily made a sitting coffin, and that evening he was placed in it. Although it was the hottest weather, his face was extraordinarily clear and handsome, and there was not the slightest odor on his body, nor a single fly. The old Dharma Master Dixian and the ordinary believers all vied with one another to see him, marveling that it was so rare. Afterwards a pyre of firewood was raised and the body was cremated; there were red flames and white smoke, and no foul odor at all. Later, when the old layman Pan Duifu heard of this, he wrote an account of Master Xiuwu's lifelong practice of Buddha-recitation, had it printed and distributed for all to see, holding him to be a fine model among monks.

The second was the layman Zheng Xibin. He was a native of Jimo in Shandong and was in business. Reading the Buddhist scriptures, he learned that Buddha-recitation was good, and so he resolved to recite the Buddha's name and never married. In the twenty-second year of the Republic (

), in Qingdao, I explained to him the three refuges and the benefits of Buddha-recitation, and from then on his recitation grew more earnest. He handed all the family affairs over to his younger brother and devoted himself single-mindedly to reciting the Buddha's name. Later he practiced until he could expound the Amitabha Sutra. Every year he would pass through Qingdao from Jimo, stay a day or two, and go on to Pingdu county to expound the sutra several times for his fellow practitioners. In the twenty-fourth year (
) Layman Zheng even invited me to Pingdu to expound the sutra once. In the spring of the twenty-eighth year (

) Layman Zheng again went by way of Qingdao to Pingdu county to expound the sutra. More than two weeks later, someone came from Pingdu county and said to me: "Old Dharma Master, do you know? Layman Zheng Xibin has gone home!" (People in eastern Shandong say of a person's death that he has "gone home.") I was quite startled to hear this. I said: "Only ten days or so ago he passed through here and was perfectly well. Why has he died so soon? What illness did he have? How did he die?" The man said: After Layman Zheng finished expounding the Amitabha Sutra, the listeners all left; only five or six of those handling affairs remained, and since they were all friends they ate lunch together. After the meal Layman Zheng asked his friend to rent him a room, saying he was going to leave. His friend said: "If you are leaving, why do you need to rent a room?" Layman Zheng said: "I am going to be reborn, and I am afraid that dying in someone else's house would be taboo." His friend said: "We have been close friends for many years. Never mind being reborn in the Buddha-land; even if you were bedridden and died in my house, that would be only right. Why look for another room? There are many here who believe in the Buddha and recite his name. If you really have assurance of rebirth, then let the people of this place who recite the Buddha's name see it, and be an example for them." Having said this, his friend cleared out two rooms in his own house and made up a bed. Layman Zheng said a few brief words of farewell to his friend, shook out his clothes, sat down cross-legged on the bed facing west, and said: "I take my leave of you all. I am going now! We have been fellow believers in the Buddha together; please recite the Buddha's name and see me on my way!" His friend, standing by, said: "At the point of death, won't you say a few gathas to leave us as a keepsake?" Layman Zheng said: "Never mind gathas. Just the way you see me now, coming and going freely, is enough; if you follow my example, that will be a fine keepsake." After he said this everyone recited the Buddha's name to see him off, and in less than a quarter of an hour he passed away with a smile. Because of this, throughout the Pingdu county area everyone knew that Buddha-recitation was good, and many people were moved to take up the faith.

At first Zheng Xibin's younger brother was unhappy to see his elder brother cast aside family and property and devote himself wholly to Buddha-recitation. Later, after his brother's repeated persuasion, he reluctantly took up the faith and recited the Buddha's name, but without much earnestness. This time, seeing with his own eyes how his brother, through Buddha-recitation, attained rebirth, knew beforehand the hour of his departure, and came and went freely, he understood that Buddha-recitation was certainly no deception, and so he too devoted himself wholeheartedly to reciting the Buddha's name. Three years later he too knew beforehand the hour of his departure and was reborn through Buddha-recitation. His final illness, however, was somewhat troublesome, not so free of suffering as his brother's passing.

The third was a laywoman of the Zhang family. She was from Qingdao and had a son and a daughter. The family was very poor, and her husband made a living pulling a rickshaw at the harbor wharf. She lived near the Zhanshan Hermitage in Qingdao, where a Buddhist study society had been established. Every Sunday I would come from Zhanshan Monastery to expound the sutras there, and after hearing the teaching the laypeople would recite the Buddha's name for the time it takes one stick of incense to burn. Through this opportunity she took refuge in the Three Jewels, heard the Buddhadharma, and came to believe in the Buddha with great sincerity. Ordinarily she recited the Buddha's name at home, and on Sundays she would take her two children to the study society to hear the sutras; when the teaching was over they would, as usual, recite the Buddha's name along with everyone else.
In the winter of the twenty-sixth year (

), one day Zhang rose early in the morning and suddenly said to her husband: "Raise the children well and get along! Today I am going to be reborn in the Buddha-land." Her husband, who had to struggle for a living and had little exposure to the Buddhadharma, glared at her and scolded: "Enough! Isn't our family's poverty suffering enough for you? Now you come dragging in this nonsense too." Having said this he paid her no more attention and went off to pull his rickshaw at the wharf. Zhang then told her two children: "Today I am going to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss! You two must listen to your father and not get into mischief." Her two children, the elder not yet ten and the younger five or six, did not understand what their mother meant, and went on running in and out of the house at play. Zhang tidied the household affairs a little, washed her face and combed her hair. As the family was poor she had no new clothes to change into, so she put on a set of old clothes that had been washed and starched, sat down cross-legged on the bed facing west, and passed away while reciting the Buddha's name. Her two children, having played outside a long time, grew hungry and came home to eat. Seeing their mother sitting on the bed with no meal cooked, they went up to call her, but she did not answer; they pushed her with their hands, but she still did not move. Only then did the two children realize that their mother was dead. They ran crying to the neighbors to tell them, and the neighbors came as soon as they heard. They saw that although Zhang had been dead a long while, her face looked as if she were still alive, and they praised the depth of her practice in reciting the Buddha's name. Later her husband came back from the wharf and wept bitterly. Because the family was poor and had no means for a funeral, the laypeople of the Buddhist study society pooled money to take care of her last affairs.

The most important thing in life is to recite the Buddha's name and be free of birth and death. In any case, each of you should, according to your own circumstances, snatch a little leisure from your busy life to sit quietly for a while and recite the Buddha's name for a set time. You can also recite silently in your mind while you are working. Otherwise, if you spend your days in lust, killing, theft, and lying, in wrongdoing and lawbreaking, creating all kinds of karma, you will inevitably fall into the three evil paths and revolve through the six realms, and your suffering will never end. The Buddha says in the Surangama Sutra:

"You owe me my life, and I repay you your debt; by this cause, through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we remain always in birth and death. You love my mind, and I cherish your form; by this cause, through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we remain always bound together. Only killing, stealing, and lust are the three roots; by this cause, the fruit of karma continues without end."

Just think, everyone, how bitter it is to create the karma of killing, stealing, and lust! I urge you all to recite the Buddha's name quickly and recite it often. As the saying goes, "One recitation of the Buddha's name increases blessing immeasurably; one bow to the Buddha erases sins as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."

blocks.text: Wei Guoxing's Free and Unhindered Rebirth

inline.s: Recorded by Master Zhixing

On March 7, 2003 (the fifth day of the second lunar month), around Focheng Monastery in Qingyi township, Mianyang city, Sichuan province, auspicious clouds gathered like a canopy, a gentle breeze blew softly, sacred birds sang, and rare fragrances drifted in waves. At noon, celestial music sounded faintly and the clouds scattered like flowers. Monastics and laypeople thronged the monastery, reciting the Buddha's name in unison. Amitabha Buddha, Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta, and the bodhisattvas of the pure ocean assembly, treading on thousand-petaled jewel lotuses, gathered in the sky above the Buddha hall; more than three hundred people saw the Buddha with their own eyes, and could not contain their emotion, so that waves of weeping rose and fell. Layman Wei Guoxing ascended the golden terrace in glory and, following the assembly of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, went joyfully to the West as he had wished.

Layman Wei Guoxing was born on May 4, 1927 (the fourth day of the fourth lunar month) in the third hamlet of Xinglong village, Qingyi township, Mianyang, Sichuan. He was honest and kind by nature and made his living as a carpenter. In 1997 he took refuge and received the precepts at Shengshui Monastery. He believed firmly in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and devoted himself to reciting the Buddha's name, single-mindedly seeking rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Toward the Buddha's teachings he was utterly sincere and reverent, never failing to do a good deed because it was small, nor doing an evil one because it was small. Whenever there was life release, sutra printing, giving, assisted recitation, or support of the monastery, any such good work, he always did as much as he could according to his means.

In 2002 he contracted cancer of the esophagus, and from then on he recited the Buddha's name even more diligently. He said that when karma obstructs a reciter of the Buddha's name, it is heavy offenses being expiated lightly; it is a test from the Buddhas and bodhisattvas, so that at the end of life rebirth may be unobstructed. When his family wanted to send him to hospital for treatment he firmly refused, saying: "If I am to stay anywhere, I will stay in Amitabha Buddha's great hospital." On this matter he once asked his teacher for guidance. Master Dexin instructed him: "At such a time you should redouble what is usual: be more single-minded and concentrated, recite the Buddha's name with vigor, let go of body and mind entirely, and with utmost sincerity and earnestness seek rebirth above all. If your allotted span is not yet exhausted, the illness will heal of itself and you will have created a miracle; if your allotted span is at an end, then this is the hour of your rebirth. At the very least you should strive to know beforehand the hour of your departure and to be received and guided by the Buddha, setting an example for reciters of the Buddha's name in ages to come, creating an even greater miracle and benefiting countless living beings." Hearing the master's instruction, his mind opened and he understood, and he broke into a radiant smile. Before the Buddha he vowed to take his illness and suffering as a contributing condition for Buddha-recitation and the quest for rebirth, to let go utterly of body, mind, and world, to recite with wholehearted devotion, and to seek with single purpose rebirth in the Land of Lotuses.
At last one day he went to Master Dexin and said: "Master, let me tell you some good news."
"What good news?" asked Master Dexin.
He said: "While I was reciting the Buddha's name, the Buddhas and bodhisattvas told me that in a few days they will come to take me to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss."

What wonderful news! How extraordinary! Hearing this, Master Dexin was overjoyed and stirred, and said to him with enthusiasm: "Since you have such skill in practice and have been personally assured by the Buddha, we ought to hold a great seven-day rebirth assembly for you, as assisted recitation to see you on your way. On the day of the assembly you may follow Amitabha Buddha, Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, and Bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta and be reborn at ease. You set the date."
"Let it be the twenty-ninth, then."
"Good, then it is settled!"
The assembly began on the twenty-ninth day of the first lunar month and ended on the fifth day of the second lunar month, lasting exactly seven days.

On the day the assembly reached its perfect conclusion he said to everyone: "I must bring this assembly to a perfect close. Why? Because many suffering beings say, 'You are always telling us that studying the Buddha's teaching is good, but where is the good in it? You say the good is freedom in birth and death, but where is the freedom? Let us see!' So I will show you. Can't be done? Students of the Buddha do not tell lies. Therefore this time I will complete the great work of studying the Buddha's teaching and show you an example. These suffering beings are deluded and confused, but just think: the thirty-two marks, the eighty subsidiary marks ..."

The day before his rebirth he himself led the assembly to a small riverside to release living creatures, and circled the Buddha and chanted with everyone. On the eve of his rebirth he addressed them all: "There are still eleven hours left." He looked down at the watch on his wrist for a while, then went on: "I am a man who loves most of all to give things up." He looked down again at the time on his watch and said: "When I went about telling people everywhere, I gave things up too, and everyone became very doubtful; they doubted the truth of the matter. 'What are you talking about? I don't believe it.' Well then, on the fifth day of this lunar month I ask you all to come and see for yourselves. Some people say, 'Is this old man out of his mind?' I say this is the real situation. I tell you, why do I do this? People of the world, you all have to give up (he said the words "give up" with great weight and earnestness) before you can put on clothes, before you can bathe, before you can cut your toenails and go (he made a gesture of helplessly letting go of the world). I, on the contrary, want to do something with a bit of form to it. Why? I have deliberately stayed alive and dwelt here for seven days. For these seven days I have been holding my seven-day Way-place in Qingyi township, Focheng district, Mianyang city. Every day I have followed along reciting sutras, bowing in repentance, circling and reciting the Buddha's name. But those who were notified to come in all came on the twenty-ninth to bow to the Buddha, bow to the sutras, and bow in repentance, because many of them came to watch the excitement, doubting what I said about the twenty-ninth. This Way-place of mine, this rebirth assembly: the opening ceremony of the first day of the seven-day Buddha-retreat, on the afternoon of the twenty-eighth, the chairman of the Sichuan Provincial Buddhist Association gave the opening address (he looked down at his watch); tomorrow, the fifth, in the afternoon the closing ceremony of the rebirth assembly will be held and it will end. I hope that none of you will think this Way-place is superstition, or some kind of trick, or some other ghostly business, or that it is organizing Falun Gong, and stir up trouble in this Way-place. You who talk wild nonsense and think Buddhism is superstition: Buddhism is education. It educates people to walk on the right track, the road to prosperity. It teaches people to do no evil, to practice all good, to be filial to their parents, and to take filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness as the foundation. Of all virtues filial piety is foremost; of all evils lust is the chief. Nowadays this society turns everything everywhere into amusement parks ..."

At ten in the morning on the fifth day of the second lunar month, two hours before the hour of Layman Wei's rebirth, he held a farewell ceremony with the more than fifteen hundred laypeople present and with those who had come to watch. The old man calmly bowed and burned incense before the Buddha in the great hall, and finally gave the assembly this instruction: "Virtuous ones, good teachers, fellow practitioners, guests, and people all: today is the day of my rebirth; the seven-day rebirth assembly has come to a complete and successful close. On this last day of farewell, thank you all for your care!" Everyone was overcome with emotion, grief and joy mingled.

Thereupon Master Dexin, together with Layman Wei's family and the assembled monastics and laypeople, escorted him as he walked slowly into the Rebirth Hall of the laymen's building. Before the Buddha he bowed in utmost reverence and took up incense, then sat upright on a wooden chair, his hands forming the Amitabha mudra, and chanted the Buddha's name aloud with the assembly. Suddenly auspicious light filled the room, with rare fragrance and wondrous music, and all who saw or smelled it felt body and mind at once peaceful and well. And when they looked again, Layman Wei Guoxing had already passed peacefully to the West, following the Buddha. Freedom in birth and death: a song without equal through the ages; the skill of Buddha-recitation had reached the very summit. Since ancient times, among the masters of the Chan gate and the teachings, learned as a forest and of immense attainment, those who freed themselves from birth and death, left the dust, escaped the wheel of suffering, and went wherever their hearts desired, even they never surpassed this height.

Layman Wei Guoxing was a carpenter in lay life, no man of lofty intelligence or remarkable gifts; in a mere three to five years he recited the Buddha's name and was born in the Buddha-land, an attainment unprecedented and unmatched, shaking heaven and earth and moving ghosts and spirits to tears. This is proof enough that the words of the Buddha and the sayings of the patriarchs are no idle boast: the foolish and the wise, the simple and the learned, need only have wholehearted faith and vows, recite the Buddha's name with sincere devotion, and seek rebirth; all attain it equally, and ten thousand practice and ten thousand arrive. Patriarch Yinguang says:

"One should make a real and earnest vow: the vow to leave the suffering of the Saha world, and the vow to attain the joy of Ultimate Bliss. Such a vow should be as urgent as that of one who has fallen into a cesspit and longs desperately to get out, or of one bound in prison who longs for home; unable to free oneself by one's own power, one must seek one of great power to pull one out."
He also says:

"Recite the single line Namo Amitabha Buddha; recite it until it is familiar, and there will be more than enough left over for attaining Buddhahood! If one studies no other dharma, what is there to regret?"

May all beings know that the light of life flashes like lightning, be wary of the perils of the road of rebirth, hold the name and recite the Buddha, and attain liberation in this very life. Namo Amitabha Buddha! Namo Amitabha Buddha! Namo Amitabha Buddha!
"Gather in the six sense faculties; let pure mindfulness continue without interruption. This is foremost."
Ah!

blocks.text: A Report Delivered After Rebirth in the Pure Land

inline.s: (Honghua Monthly, July 1944, issue 37, "News Reported After Rebirth in the West")

Layman Zhu's given name was Dingyi; his courtesy name was Jingchen, and he also used the courtesy name Xingwu. He was a native of Kunming in Yunnan and practiced medicine for a living; in his spare time he often practiced quiet sitting at his leisure.

was the year when, at the urging of his close friend Layman Wang Jueru, he turned to the practice of Buddha-recitation and made considerable progress. The following summer he caught a cold and took to his bed. Wang Jueru came to visit and urged him to go and rest at the famous Yunqi Monastery outside the city, where he could also hear expositions of the Surangama Sutra, and he accompanied him there. Ten days later Zhu Dingyi returned home, and Wang Jueru went to see him again and found him gravely ill and suffering from diarrhea. So he advised him: "You are a doctor and can diagnose and treat yourself. But now that your illness has grown this serious, I feel that your own diagnosis and treatment are probably not correct. Why not call in another doctor to examine and treat you, so that you may recover sooner?" Layman Zhu said: "No, no. After you all went to hear the sutra, one night I dreamed that I saw Amitabha Buddha, and in my joy I bowed to him. Just as I was prostrating myself fully, I also saw the Great Being in White Robes, also of very tall stature, coming toward me face to face. As he drew near, fearing that his robes might brush against me, he lifted the hem of his garment and passed quietly by my side, a smile on his face. Judging by this, it seems he is about to receive and guide me to the West. Why should I call in a doctor again?" Before long his illness grew worse, and knowing that his hour had come, he asked Wang Jueru to invite monks on his behalf to come to his house for assisted recitation. And so on the night of the sixth day of the sixth month he sat cross-legged and passed away while reciting the Buddha's name.

When Wang Jueru had invited the monks to come and recite the Buddha's name, Layman Zhu said: "Tonight I will certainly be reborn." Wang Jueru was half believing and half doubting, and so he made a pact with him: "Nowadays the matter of attaining rebirth in the West through Buddha-recitation rests only on the auspicious signs at the moment of death. And after one has been born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss there is no other firm evidence either. If you are reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss this time, you must come back in person to report it, and prove that you really have been reborn there. Be sure to remember this!" Layman Zhu said: "How shall I report it?" Wang Jueru said: "Have you not seen in the books the story of Que Gongze, who was reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and came back to report it?" Layman Zhu said: "That manner of reporting requires the highest grade of the highest birth; how could I manage that? I can only report in a dream." Wang Jueru said: "That is fine too. As long as it proves that you have been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, that will do."

[Que Gongze] The Biographies of Lay Buddhists records: Que Gongze was a man of Hebei. In the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty he lived in Luoyang, where his life was leisured and joyful, free and unconstrained, and he regularly recited the Lotus Sutra of the Correct Dharma. After Que Gongze's rebirth, his friends held an assembly for him at the White Horse Monastery in Luoyang. When evening came and the sutra was being recited, a voice was suddenly heard in the air. The assembly looked up and saw a person whose body and countenance were bright and beautiful, who said: "I am Que Gongze. I have already been born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, and now, together with the supremely good people there, I have come here to hear the sutra." Everyone in the hall saw this sight. There was a man named Wei Shidu who lived in Jijun and was a disciple of Que Gongze; his mother often offered vegetarian meals to monks. That same day, toward noon, a bowl suddenly descended from the sky and landed right in front of Wei's mother. Examining it closely, they saw that it was the very bowl Que Gongze had always used, and it was filled with rice whose fragrance filled the whole hall. Everyone who ate the rice from the bowl went seven days without hunger. The eminent Jin-dynasty monk Zhi Daolin praised this event without end. [Lotus Sutra of the Correct Dharma] Translated by Dharmaraksha in the Western Jin, it is the earliest translation of the Lotus Sutra.

After Layman Zhu passed away sitting, his body was placed in a coffin according to Buddhist custom and then cremated, and his ashes were enshrined in a stupa. By the time all this was done it was mid-sixth month. Time flowed swiftly by, and in a twinkling the seventh, eighth, and ninth months had all passed, yet there was not the faintest word. We began to think that Layman Zhu had not attained rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, or else that he had attained rebirth but was unwilling to communicate with us, since the promised report had never come. Then, unexpectedly, at the end of the winter month (the eleventh lunar month), Wang Jueru was lying in bed during the day because of a toothache. In a daze he saw Layman Zhu come upstairs and sit down on a stool. (Original note: Mr. Wang Jueru, being devoted to Buddha-recitation, had his bed placed beside the Buddha hall upstairs.) His body was as it had been before. He wore a half-new flat-topped cap and a garment that looked as if it had been washed; both were very clean, and a radiance shone from them. His bearing was vivacious and his face like the full moon, while his skin was so fine and smooth that he looked like a handsome boy of eight. Compared with the bearded face, missing teeth, and wrinkled skin of his former years, he was a different person altogether. Had Wang Jueru not been his closest friend, thoroughly familiar with him, and a boon companion from childhood, he would scarcely have recognized him. For such beauty and grace had never been Layman Zhu's in all his life.

At the sight of him Wang Jueru was overjoyed beyond measure and spoke incoherently, asking urgently: "Oh! Have you really been born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss? Otherwise, how could you have such grace? You do not know how you look now: you are altogether a handsome, delicate boy. In life you had lost more than half your teeth; I once asked you to go to the Songzhu Residence to have false teeth made. Do you remember?" Layman Zhu said: "Yes, yes. I have come expressly to report to you." Wang Jueru said: "The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands away; it is very hard to come back here, yet you have come." He answered: "The only reason I could come back here is the power of faith and vows." Wang Jueru said: "How did you come back here?" He answered: "Very easily. One thought and I arrived. In the future you will know for yourself. When you want to come back, look toward the dark; when you want to return to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, look toward the light. That is how it is." Wang Jueru asked again: "Have you seen the Buddha?" He answered: "No, I have not." Wang Jueru asked: "Why can you not see him?" He answered: "My practice is too shallow; I did not attain birth in the seven-jeweled pond." Wang Jueru asked: "If not in the seven-jeweled pond, then where were you born?" Layman Zhu sighed and said: "Alas, the place where I was born is only the ground of the West. A borderland, I suppose."

Before the conversation ended, Wang Jueru suddenly awoke. Opening his eyes he recalled it: Layman Zhu's words and bearing, his radiance and noble marks, were vivid before him, in no way comparable to a confused dream. He rose and looked at the clock; it was a little past five in the afternoon. A month later, with winter over and spring come round again, Wang Jueru happened to meet Wang Nengzhi, a close relative of Layman Zhu by marriage. As soon as they met, Wang Nengzhi said to him in haste: "How strange! Last winter Zhu Xingwu came several times to talk with me, saying that he had been reborn in the borderland of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and had come especially to report it. I have been wanting to visit you and tell you all this." Wang Jueru eagerly asked him what Layman Zhu had said. Wang Nengzhi recounted: "As soon as I saw him I asked: 'Where have you been these past months, and why did you not come back sooner to report?' Layman Zhu answered: 'I had business in the underworld that delayed me a long while. Thanks to Bodhisattva Ksitigarbha, who sent someone to escort me, I was able to find time to come.' He also said: 'In life I gave you books on Buddha-recitation; have you put them into practice? You used to run a restaurant and slaughtered many creatures; your offenses are very heavy. From now on, besides reciting the Buddha's name diligently, you must repent all the more, and you must eat vegetarian food and strictly refrain from killing. Rebirth in the West is the portion of everyone and is very easy; do not cast yourself away in despair. I deeply regret that I began reciting the Buddha's name too late and that my practice was too poor. You would do well to begin your own practice early.' And so on." After Layman Zhu's report, Wang Jueru's friends who heard of it all urged him to write it out and publish it, to awaken people's faith. So Wang Jueru wrote it down plainly according to the facts. At the end of the manuscript he added: "I solemnly swear by the precepts that there is not one false word, nor have I added or subtracted a single character from Mr. Zhu's answers in the dream." Yesterday he sent the manuscript by special mail to this journal, asking that it be published. We now publish his manuscript to inform monastics and laypeople throughout the country.
Layman Zhu Dingyi, courtesy name Jingchen, also Xingwu, was a man of Kunming in Yunnan. He practiced medicine, and in his leisure often practiced quiet sitting.

was the year when, at the urging of his close friend Layman Wang Jueru, he turned to the practice of Buddha-recitation and made considerable progress. The following summer he caught a cold and lay confined to bed. Mr. Wang went to see him and urged him to go to the

famous Yunqi Monastery to rest, and also to hear the Surangama Sutra expounded, and he accompanied him there. Ten days later he returned, and Mr. Wang went again to see him, and found that his illness was accompanied by diarrhea. He advised him, saying: "Though you practice medicine and can diagnose and treat yourself, now that your illness has come to this, I fear your own sense and judgment may be at fault. Why not call in another doctor for an examination, so that you may recover sooner?" The layman said: "No, no. After you all went to hear the sutra, one night I dreamed that I saw Amitabha Buddha, and in my joy I made obeisance. Just as I was prostrating myself fully, I again saw the Great Being in White Robes, also of tall stature, coming toward me face to face. As he drew near, fearing that his robe might brush against me, he lifted his garment with his hand and passed quietly by my side, a smile on his face. Judging by this, it seems he will receive and guide me to the West; what need is there to call a doctor for another examination?" Before long his illness grew worse, and knowing his hour had come, he asked Mr. Wang to invite monks on his behalf to his house for assisted recitation. And so on the night of the sixth day of the sixth month he passed away sitting cross-legged while reciting the Buddha's name.
[Kou (kou) yi] To lift the hem of a garment.

When Mr. Wang had invited monks on his behalf to come and recite the Buddha's name, the layman said of himself: "Tonight I shall certainly go." Mr. Wang was half doubtful and half believing, and so made a pact with him, saying: "Nowadays the matter of attaining rebirth in the West through Buddha-recitation rests only on the auspicious signs at the moment of death. And after one has been born in the West there is no other firm proof either. If you are born in the West this time, you must come in person to report it, and prove it truly and conclusively. Be sure to remember this." The layman said: "How shall I report it?" Mr. Wang said: "Have you not seen how the books record the matter of Que Gongze, who was born in the West and reported it?" The layman said: "That manner of reporting requires the highest grade of the highest birth; how could I do that? I can only report it in a dream." Mr. Wang said: "That is fine too; so long as it proves the matter, it will do."

[Que Gongze] The Biographies of Lay Buddhists says: "Que Gongze was a man of Zhao. In the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin he lived in Luoyang, utterly detached and serene, and daily recited the Lotus Sutra of the Correct Dharma. After he died, his friends held an assembly for him at the White Horse Monastery, and when evening came they recited the sutra. Suddenly a voice was heard in the air; looking up, they saw a person of bright and beautiful appearance, who said: 'I am Que Gongze. I have been born in the Western Land of Peace and Bliss, and together with the supreme beings I have come here to hear the sutra.' Everyone in the hall saw him. There was a man of Jijun named Wei Shidu, who had studied under Gongze, and whose mother often fed monks. That day toward noon a bowl suddenly fell from the sky and landed right in front of his mother. Examining it closely, it was the bowl Gongze had always used, filled with rice, whose fragrance filled the hall; those who ate of it went seven days without hunger. Zhi Daolin wrote a praise for him, saying: 'Great indeed was Que Gong, who savored emptiness and received the spirit; his divine transformation crossed to the Western Regions, his traces answered in the Eastern Capital; he lingered in the ethereal heights, sent forth his sound and made his form shine. How could a single praise suffice? He showed thereby that he is not among the shadowed dead.'"

After he sat upright and passed away, in accordance with the Buddha's rule he was placed in a shrine, cremated, and his ashes placed in a stupa. When all these matters were done it was already the middle of the sixth month. Time flew like a galloping horse, and in a flash the seventh, eighth, and ninth months passed, yet there was no news at all. I privately supposed that the layperson had not been reborn in the West, or that having been reborn there he was unwilling to communicate with us, so that the agreement we had made could not be fulfilled. But contrary
(unexpectedly)
to expectations, at the end of the eleventh month

on one day, Mr. Wang, owing to a toothache, lay down to rest upon his bed in the daytime. In a drowse he saw the layperson ascend the stairs and sit upon a stool. (Original note: Because Mr. Wang practiced Buddha-recitation, his bed was placed beside the recitation hall upstairs.) His frame was as before, wearing a nearly new flat-topped hat and clothes that seemed to have been freshly washed — all clean, with a radiance emanating from them. His spirit was bright and untrammeled, his face like the full moon. His skin was tender and delicate, like that of a handsome eight-year-old boy. Compared with his living face, full of moustache and beard
(whiskers)
, with teeth fallen out and skin wrinkled, he was as if a different man. Had Mr. Wang not been his closest friend, acquainted
(intimately familiar)
with him to the fullest, and moreover a childhood friend of the same village
(a friend made in boyhood)
, he would hardly have been able to recognize him. For this beautiful bearing was something the layperson had never had in all his life.
At the first sight Mr. Wang was extraordinarily startled and delighted, and spoke without order, hastily
(abruptly)

asking: ‘Ah! Have you in truth been reborn in the West? If not, how could you have such grace? You do not know how your face now is — altogether a tender, handsome boy. When you were alive most of your teeth had fallen; I once promised you to go to Pine and Bamboo Studio to have your teeth set. Do you still remember?’ The layperson said: ‘Yes, yes, I have made a point of coming to tell you the news.’ Mr. Wang said: ‘The West is one hundred thousand million Buddha-lands away from here; it is not easy to reach at all. How did you manage to get there?’ He answered: ‘That I got there was entirely the power of faith and vow.’ Mr. Wang said: ‘How were you able to go?’ He answered: ‘Very easy — at the very raising of a single thought I was there. In time you will know for yourself. Only, when coming, look toward the dark place, and when going, look toward the bright place — that is all.’ Mr. Wang asked again: ‘Have you seen the Buddha?’ He answered: ‘Not yet.’ He asked: ‘Why could you not see him?’ He answered: ‘My merit and practice were too shallow, so I was not born in the pool of the seven jewels.’ He asked: ‘Not born in the pool of the seven jewels — then where were you born?’ The layperson sighed: ‘Alas, the place I went to was only the ground of the West. Ah, I suppose it counts as the borderlands.’

Before the conversation was finished, of a sudden he woke. Opening his eyes and recalling, he felt that the layperson's speech and bearing, and the radiant mark and good form, stood clearly before his eyes — in no way to be compared to the inverted thoughts of a dream. Rising to look at the clock, it was just a little past five in the afternoon. A month later
(after a month had passed)

, when the twelfth month had ended and spring had returned, Mr. Wang chanced to meet the layperson's relative Wang Nengzhi. The moment they met, Nengzhi at once said to Mr. Wang: ‘Strange! Last winter Zhu Xingwu came several times to talk with me, saying that he had attained the borderlands of the West and had come specially to deliver the news. I have long wished to visit you to tell you of it all.’ Mr. Wang, eagerly
(urgently)

finding out what he had said, Nengzhi related: ‘The moment I saw him I asked: Where did you go these past few months? Why did you not come earlier? The layperson answered: Because I had some business in the underworld, I was delayed a long while. Thanks to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva's sending someone to escort me, I was only then able to spare a moment to come. He also said: When I was alive I gave you books on Buddha-recitation — did you put them into practice? In the past you ran an eatery and did much slaughter; your wrongdoing is very heavy. From now on, besides earnestly reciting the Buddha-name, you must further repent, become a vegetarian, and strictly observe the precept against killing. As for rebirth in the West, everyone has a share in it; it is very easy, so do not on any account give yourself up. I greatly regret that I began to recite too late and that my merit was too poor; you should begin your practice early — that is the point, and so on.’ After the layperson had delivered the news, Mr. Wang's friends, hearing of it, urged him to record it to awaken people's faith. Mr. Wang thereupon wrote it out directly as the matter had occurred. And in an afterword he wrote: ‘I solemnly swear by my precepts that there is not a single false word, and that I have not changed a single word, more or less, of what Mr. Zhu said in the dream.’ Recently he sent a letter to this journal and asked that it be published. All now relate this account, to inform the monastics and laypeople of the whole country.

The power of example is boundless! The above examples of free and unhindered rebirth are immensely inspiring and also give one much to ponder. Han Yu, in his essay On the Root of Fault-Finding, has a passage telling people how to use examples to improve themselves:

“I heard that among the ancients there was one Shun, and in his way of being he was a man of benevolence and righteousness. Seeking the principle by which Shun became Shun, one blames oneself, saying: ‘He is a man; I too am a man. He was able to be this, and can I not be this?’ Morning and night one ponders, discarding what is not like Shun and taking up what is like Shun.”

(Vernacular: I hear that among the ancients there was one called Shun, and his conduct was that of a man of benevolence and righteousness. Having found the principle by which Shun became Shun, one blames oneself, saying: ‘He is a man, and I too am a man; he was able to be thus, am I then unable to be thus?’ So morning and night one thinks of how to catch up — discarding those places where one is not like Shun, and imitating those places where one is like Shun.)

When we read these examples of free rebirth, we too should thus blame ourselves, and ponder morning and night, discarding what is not like them and taking up what is like them. Yet in the accounts of free rebirth handed down through the ages, often there is only the matter of the deed, without setting forth the state he had reached before his passing, or how he came to that state — making it hard for people to emulate;
this is indeed a matter of great regret!

Take the matter of “Wei Guoxing's free rebirth” as an example. He had been reciting the Buddha's name only a mere three or five years when he foresaw that he would pass away at noon, twelve o'clock, seven days later. So he informed the practice-place in advance, and the practice-place held a grand seven-day Dharma-gathering of rebirth-and-Buddha for more than fifteen hundred people, chanting to see him off. If in these seven days someone had carefully questioned him about the state he had reached at that time, and how he had come to that state, and published it to the world, how immense would have been the help to those practicing Buddha-recitation!

I earnestly hope that those so fortunate as to meet in the future a person who foresees the time of his passing will carefully question him as to his state and how he reached it, and make it known to all, for the benefit of the practitioners of Buddha-recitation in all ages to come. If a practitioner of Buddha-recitation has foreknowledge of his time, then before he passes away let him, with a bodhi-mind, tell his fellow practitioners his concrete methods of study and practice, the process, and the states he attained, together with his experiences and lessons — or write them up for publication — and thus, before the fulfillment of his vow to return, broadly ferry sentient beings across.
